title: CYSTINOSIS, LATE-ONSET JUVENILE OR ADOLESCENT NEPHROPATHIC TYPE

relationships.phenotype: CYSTINOSIS, LATE-ONSET JUVENILE OR ADOLESCENT NEPHROPATHIC TYPE

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CTNS gene.

checks.claim: Late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis is caused by homozygous mutation in the CTNS gene.
checks.evidence_quote: The disease occurs due either to the combination of one mild mutation and one which is known to cause nephropathic cystinosis or to homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation.
checks.explanation: The abstract names homozygosity for a mild CTNS mutation as one cause of intermediate cystinosis. 'Intermediate' is a synonym for the late-onset juvenile/adolescent form.

checks.claim: Late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the CTNS gene.
checks.evidence_quote: The disease occurs due either to the combination of one mild mutation and one which is known to cause nephropathic cystinosis or to homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation.
checks.explanation: One mild mutation combined with one nephropathic mutation is compound heterozygosity in CTNS.

paragraphs.text: Late-onset cystinosis is rarer than infantile nephropathic cystinosis. Attard et al. (1999) noted that its symptoms begin between 12 and 15 years of age. Renal failure has been reported in affected sibs (Langman et al., 1985). The disorder is caused by mutations in the CTNS gene, which encodes cystinosin. These mutations are thought to be milder than those that cause the infantile nephropathic form (Thoene et al., 1999; Attard et al., 1999).

paragraphs.text: Attard et al. (1999) described 3 patients whose cystinosis began before 7 years of age but whose disease course was milder than the infantile nephropathic form. The authors suggested that the missense mutations found in these patients allow production of functional protein. They also suggested that these mutations may mark regions of cystinosin that are not functionally important.

paragraphs.text: Thoene et al. (1999) described 6 patients with the intermediate form of cystinosis who had mutations in the CTNS gene, 2 of them new. In some patients, a mild mutation was combined with a mutation known to cause nephropathic cystinosis. In others, a predicted mild mutation was homozygous. Thoene et al. (1999) transfected cystinotic fibroblasts with either normal CTNS cDNA or a cDNA carrying a mutation that causes intermediate cystinosis. Both partly corrected the cystinotic phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Attard et al. (1999) screened the CTNS gene in patients with infantile nephropathic cystinosis, patients with late-onset cystinosis, and patients whose phenotype did not fit the classical definitions. They found 23 different CTNS mutations, 14 of them novel. In 2 patients with late-onset cystinosis, the mutations affected regions of cystinosin that are not functionally important. The authors said this accounts for the milder phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Attard et al. (1999) studied 25 patients with infantile nephropathic cystinosis. Twelve had 2 severely truncating CTNS mutations, consistent with loss of functional protein. The other 13 had missense mutations or in-frame deletions that were predicted to disrupt transmembrane domains of cystinosin and cause loss of protein function. In contrast, the mutations in patients with late-onset disease affected regions of the protein that are not functionally important.
